Croupier · Privé Blackjack · Commercial treatment v2
The Table Is Yours
30-second hero spot and Higgsfield production plan. One private salon, one dealer who talks back — and mid-sentence, she is someone else. The dealer swap is the spot.
30s hero · 15s · 6s bumper21:9 / 16:9 / 9:16Voice: Vera
1Concept
Every other casino ad sells noise. This one sells the opposite: a private salon, one dealer, and she talks back. Then, mid-sentence, she is someone else.
The dealer changes while she speaks — same frame, same light, same voice, a different woman on each hard cut — because on this product the dealer is a choice, not a fixture. The ad doesn't describe the feature; it performs it.
Tone: restrained, expensive, a little cold. A watch commercial that happens to have cards in it. No hype VO, no "WIN BIG." Vera underplays everything. Two things to remember: the dealer talks back, and the dealer is yours to choose.
2The device — one sentence, three dealers
She begins a sentence. On a hard cut she is a different dealer — identical framing, lighting, posture — finishing the same sentence without a hitch. Three characters, cuts accelerating, landing back on Vera:
"Your table⟋is open⟋whenever⟋you want it."
Cut 1 (~1.2s in): Vera → Dealer Two
Cut 2 (~0.8s later): Dealer Two → Dealer Three
Cut 3 (~0.5s later): Dealer Three → Vera, who lands the sentence and the brand
The audience gets it on the second cut and grins on the third.
The rule that sells the illusion
ONE continuous VO take across all four segments. Only the picture changes; every clip is laid against that single audio track. If each dealer speaks her own take, the rhythm breaks and it reads as four ads stitched together.

Commercial script and Higgsfield production plan
Product: Croupier — Privé Blackjack, AI live dealer Formats: 30s hero · 15s cutdown · 6s bumper Aspect: 21:9 hero / 16:9 delivery / 9:16 social Voice: Vera (the dealer). She narrates her own table.
1. Concept
Every other casino ad sells noise: confetti, coins, a stranger shouting about jackpots. This one sells the opposite of noise. A private salon. One dealer. She knows your name, she answers when you speak, and she is watched.
The through-line is arrival: an empty room becomes your room. The spot ends where the product actually lives — a table that opens at 4am with nobody else in it.
Tone: restrained, expensive, a little cold. Think a watch commercial that happens to have cards in it. No hype VO, no "WIN BIG". Vera underplays everything.
The one thing to remember: the dealer talks back.

11.1 Scope first — do not edit the whole 30s
The panel is showing Whole video 0:00 - 0:30, Selection is over 30s, 195 credits. An edit model applied across a whole timeline re-touches every frame it can see: it drifts the face, shifts the grade and can undo good clips to satisfy a note about one of them.
Select only the clip that has the problem, then prompt. Cheaper, and far more likely to land. The hands/pronunciation note applies to the speaking clip alone.
11.2 The fix prompt — hands and pronunciation
Scope: the speaking clip only.
Keep the shot, framing, camera, lighting, grade and background exactly as they are.
Two corrections only:
1. HANDS: her forearms and hands rest ON TOP of the green felt, clearly visible above
   the table edge, fingers relaxed and lightly interlocked on the surface. They are
   currently hidden below the table line. Bring them up onto the felt.
2. DICTION: she currently says "blackback". She must say "BLACK-JACK" - two distinct
   syllables, hard J on the second. Re-time her mouth shapes to match the corrected word.
Do not change her face, hair, uniform, the table, the room, or the camera move.
The closing "do not change" line matters. Edit models treat an unconstrained prompt as licence to reinterpret the shot.
11.3 The pronunciation is an AUDIO bug, not a video bug
If "blackback" is baked into the generated audio, asking the video model to fix it is the long way round — it has to repair the waveform and the lips together, and it usually settles for lips that fit the wrong word.
Faster and repeatable:
Regenerate that line alone with text2speech_v2, variant: "elevenlabs", spelling it "black jack" as two words so the model stops eliding it. If it still slurs, try "blak-JAK".
Feed the returned TTS job id straight into audio_references on a fresh generation of the shot — no upload step.
Now the lips are generated against correct audio instead of being patched after the fact.
Use 11.2's hand note in that same regeneration and you fix both in one pass.
12. "Choose your dealer" — the live model switch
Kevin's vision: zoom out, more casino tables, pick your influencer, the dealer changing mid-sentence.
This is the strongest idea in the project so far, because it is not a gimmick — it is the product. Multiple dealer personas on one table is a feature, and the ad demonstrates it instead of describing it.
It is also not an edit. No edit prompt turns one dealer into five. These are separate generations, cut together on the beat.
12.1 The device
She begins a sentence. On a hard cut she is a different woman — same frame, same light, same posture, same voice — finishing the same sentence without a hitch. Do it three times, accelerating: 1.2s, 0.8s, 0.5s. The audience gets it on the second cut and grins on the third.
The sentence has to be long enough to carry the cuts:
"Your table / is open / whenever / you want it."
Cut on each /. One continuous VO take across all four; only the picture changes. Generate the VO once, then lay every clip against that single audio track — that is what sells the illusion. If each dealer speaks her own take, the rhythm breaks and it reads as four ads stitched together.

Commercial script and Higgsfield production plan
Product: Croupier — Privé Blackjack, AI live dealer Formats: 30s hero · 15s cutdown · 6s bumper Aspect: 21:9 hero / 16:9 delivery / 9:16 social Voice: Vera (the dealer). She narrates her own table.
1. Concept
Every other casino ad sells noise: confetti, coins, a stranger shouting about jackpots. This one sells the opposite of noise. A private salon. One dealer. She knows your name, she answers when you speak, and she is watched.
The through-line is arrival: an empty room becomes your room. The spot ends where the product actually lives — a table that opens at 4am with nobody else in it.
Tone: restrained, expensive, a little cold. Think a watch commercial that happens to have cards in it. No hype VO, no "WIN BIG". Vera underplays everything.
The one thing to remember: the dealer talks back.

5. Full VO script (clean read)
Good evening. Your table's been waiting. Seven seats. Blackjack. Pays three to two. And someone always watching me. I don't have a tell. I don't have a bad night. Five dollars. Or five hundred thousand. Your call. Croupier. The table is yours.
Runtime at natural pace: ~19s of speech across 30s of picture. The gaps are deliberate — let shots 1, 5 and 7 breathe.
Delivery direction: Low, level, unhurried. She is not selling; she is opening a door. Never bright, never salesy. Slight warmth on "Good evening" and "The table is yours", flat and dry on "I don't have a bad night."
TTS: text2speech_v2 with variant: "elevenlabs". Generate each line as its own job and feed the job ids straight into audio_references on the matching seedance shot — no upload step needed. Match the voice already used for the in-game bank so the commercial and the product are the same person.

11. Cinema Studio edit prompts (paste-ready)
11.1 Scope first — do not edit the whole 30s
The panel is showing Whole video 0:00 - 0:30, Selection is over 30s, 195 credits. An edit model applied across a whole timeline re-touches every frame it can see: it drifts the face, shifts the grade and can undo good clips to satisfy a note about one of them.
Select only the clip that has the problem, then prompt. Cheaper, and far more likely to land. The hands/pronunciation note applies to the speaking clip alone.
11.2 The fix prompt — hands and pronunciation
Scope: the speaking clip only.
Keep the shot, framing, camera, lighting, grade and background exactly as they are.
Two corrections only:
1. HANDS: her forearms and hands rest ON TOP of the green felt, clearly visible above
   the table edge, fingers relaxed and lightly interlocked on the surface. They are
   currently hidden below the table line. Bring them up onto the felt.
2. DICTION: she currently says "blackback". She must say "BLACK-JACK" - two distinct
   syllables, hard J on the second. Re-time her mouth shapes to match the corrected word.
Do not change her face, hair, uniform, the table, the room, or the camera move.
The closing "do not change" line matters. Edit models treat an unconstrained prompt as licence to reinterpret the shot.
11.3 The pronunciation is an AUDIO bug, not a video bug
If "blackback" is baked into the generated audio, asking the video model to fix it is the long way round — it has to repair the waveform and the lips together, and it usually settles for lips that fit the wrong word.
Faster and repeatable:
Regenerate that line alone with text2speech_v2, variant: "elevenlabs", spelling it "black jack" as two words so the model stops eliding it. If it still slurs, try "blak-JAK".
Feed the returned TTS job id straight into audio_references on a fresh generation of the shot — no upload step.
Now the lips are generated against correct audio instead of being patched after the fact.
Use 11.2's hand note in that same regeneration and you fix both in one pass.
12. "Choose your dealer" — the live model switch
Kevin's vision: zoom out, more casino tables, pick your influencer, the dealer changing mid-sentence.
This is the strongest idea in the project so far, because it is not a gimmick — it is the product. Multiple dealer personas on one table is a feature, and the ad demonstrates it instead of describing it.
It is also not an edit. No edit prompt turns one dealer into five. These are separate generations, cut together on the beat.
12.1 The device
She begins a sentence. On a hard cut she is a different woman — same frame, same light, same posture, same voice — finishing the same sentence without a hitch. Do it three times, accelerating: 1.2s, 0.8s, 0.5s. The audience gets it on the second cut and grins on the third.
The sentence has to be long enough to carry the cuts:
"Your table / is open / whenever / you want it."
Cut on each /. One continuous VO take across all four; only the picture changes. Generate the VO once, then lay every clip against that single audio track — that is what sells the illusion. If each dealer speaks her own take, the rhythm breaks and it reads as four ads stitched together.
12.2 Per-dealer generation template
Generate one per persona. Change only the bracketed description. Every other word stays byte-identical, or the cuts will jump.
Locked-off medium shot, camera completely static, no push, no drift.
A [PERSONA] casino dealer in a crisp white shirt, black waistcoat and black bow tie
stands behind a green baize blackjack table in a warm mahogany private salon. Brass wall
sconces and navy velvet curtains behind her. Her forearms rest on the felt, hands lightly
interlocked on the table surface, clearly above the table edge.
She is speaking directly to camera, mid-sentence, natural mouth movement, relaxed and
confident. Warm key from above, soft rim from the sconces.
85mm look, shallow depth of field, cinematic, film grain. Identical framing and identical
lighting in every version.
[PERSONA] swaps, for example: auburn-haired woman in her late twenties · Black woman in her thirties with short natural hair · East Asian woman with a sleek dark ponytail · older silver-haired man with a trimmed beard.
Framing discipline is everything. Same lens, same eyeline height, same distance to the felt, same head position in frame. If one dealer sits 40px lower the cut becomes a jolt instead of a swap. Generate all of them in one sitting with the same seed settings.
12.3 The pull-back reveal
Immediately after the last swap, go wide and show why:
Continuous smooth dolly back with a slight crane up, starting behind one blackjack table
and pulling out to reveal a vast opulent casino salon floor: a dozen more blackjack tables
in receding rows, a different dealer standing at each one, warm brass sconces and navy
velvet curtains throughout, deep perspective, volumetric haze in the lamplight.
Anamorphic 21:9, cinematic, single continuous take, no cuts.
Text: EVERY TABLE. EVERY DEALER. YOUR CALL. VO (Vera): "Pick one."

5. Full VO script (clean read)
Good evening. Your table's been waiting. Seven seats. Blackjack. Pays three to two. And someone always watching me. I don't have a tell. I don't have a bad night. Five dollars. Or five hundred thousand. Your call. Croupier. The table is yours.
Runtime at natural pace: ~19s of speech across 30s of picture. The gaps are deliberate — let shots 1, 5 and 7 breathe.
Delivery direction: Low, level, unhurried. She is not selling; she is opening a door. Never bright, never salesy. Slight warmth on "Good evening" and "The table is yours", flat and dry on "I don't have a bad night."
TTS: text2speech_v2 with variant: "elevenlabs". Generate each line as its own job and feed the job ids straight into audio_references on the matching seedance shot — no upload step needed. Match the voice already used for the in-game bank so the commercial and the product are the same person.

11. Cinema Studio edit prompts (paste-ready)
11.1 Scope first — do not edit the whole 30s
The panel is showing Whole video 0:00 - 0:30, Selection is over 30s, 195 credits. An edit model applied across a whole timeline re-touches every frame it can see: it drifts the face, shifts the grade and can undo good clips to satisfy a note about one of them.
Select only the clip that has the problem, then prompt. Cheaper, and far more likely to land. The hands/pronunciation note applies to the speaking clip alone.
11.2 The fix prompt — hands and pronunciation
Scope: the speaking clip only.
Keep the shot, framing, camera, lighting, grade and background exactly as they are.
Two corrections only:
1. HANDS: her forearms and hands rest ON TOP of the green felt, clearly visible above
   the table edge, fingers relaxed and lightly interlocked on the surface. They are
   currently hidden below the table line. Bring them up onto the felt.
2. DICTION: she currently says "blackback". She must say "BLACK-JACK" - two distinct
   syllables, hard J on the second. Re-time her mouth shapes to match the corrected word.
Do not change her face, hair, uniform, the table, the room, or the camera move.
The closing "do not change" line matters. Edit models treat an unconstrained prompt as licence to reinterpret the shot.
11.3 The pronunciation is an AUDIO bug, not a video bug
If "blackback" is baked into the generated audio, asking the video model to fix it is the long way round — it has to repair the waveform and the lips together, and it usually settles for lips that fit the wrong word.
Faster and repeatable:
Regenerate that line alone with text2speech_v2, variant: "elevenlabs", spelling it "black jack" as two words so the model stops eliding it. If it still slurs, try "blak-JAK".
Feed the returned TTS job id straight into audio_references on a fresh generation of the shot — no upload step.
Now the lips are generated against correct audio instead of being patched after the fact.
Use 11.2's hand note in that same regeneration and you fix both in one pass.
12. "Choose your dealer" — the live model switch
Kevin's vision: zoom out, more casino tables, pick your influencer, the dealer changing mid-sentence.
This is the strongest idea in the project so far, because it is not a gimmick — it is the product. Multiple dealer personas on one table is a feature, and the ad demonstrates it instead of describing it.
It is also not an edit. No edit prompt turns one dealer into five. These are separate generations, cut together on the beat.
12.1 The device
She begins a sentence. On a hard cut she is a different woman — same frame, same light, same posture, same voice — finishing the same sentence without a hitch. Do it three times, accelerating: 1.2s, 0.8s, 0.5s. The audience gets it on the second cut and grins on the third.
The sentence has to be long enough to carry the cuts:
"Your table / is open / whenever / you want it."
Cut on each /. One continuous VO take across all four; only the picture changes. Generate the VO once, then lay every clip against that single audio track — that is what sells the illusion. If each dealer speaks her own take, the rhythm breaks and it reads as four ads stitched together.
12.2 Per-dealer generation template
Generate one per persona. Change only the bracketed description. Every other word stays byte-identical, or the cuts will jump.
Locked-off medium shot, camera completely static, no push, no drift.
A [PERSONA] casino dealer in a crisp white shirt, black waistcoat and black bow tie
stands behind a green baize blackjack table in a warm mahogany private salon. Brass wall
sconces and navy velvet curtains behind her. Her forearms rest on the felt, hands lightly
interlocked on the table surface, clearly above the table edge.
She is speaking directly to camera, mid-sentence, natural mouth movement, relaxed and
confident. Warm key from above, soft rim from the sconces.
85mm look, shallow depth of field, cinematic, film grain. Identical framing and identical
lighting in every version.
[PERSONA] swaps, for example: auburn-haired woman in her late twenties · Black woman in her thirties with short natural hair · East Asian woman with a sleek dark ponytail · older silver-haired man with a trimmed beard.
Framing discipline is everything. Same lens, same eyeline height, same distance to the felt, same head position in frame. If one dealer sits 40px lower the cut becomes a jolt instead of a swap. Generate all of them in one sitting with the same seed settings.
12.3 The pull-back reveal
Immediately after the last swap, go wide and show why:
Continuous smooth dolly back with a slight crane up, starting behind one blackjack table
and pulling out to reveal a vast opulent casino salon floor: a dozen more blackjack tables
in receding rows, a different dealer standing at each one, warm brass sconces and navy
velvet curtains throughout, deep perspective, volumetric haze in the lamplight.
Anamorphic 21:9, cinematic, single continuous take, no cuts.
Text: EVERY TABLE. EVERY DEALER. YOUR CALL. VO (Vera): "Pick one."

5. Full VO script (clean read)
Good evening. Your table's been waiting. Seven seats. Blackjack. Pays three to two. And someone always watching me. I don't have a tell. I don't have a bad night. Five dollars. Or five hundred thousand. Your call. Croupier. The table is yours.
Runtime at natural pace: ~19s of speech across 30s of picture. The gaps are deliberate — let shots 1, 5 and 7 breathe.
Delivery direction: Low, level, unhurried. She is not selling; she is opening a door. Never bright, never salesy. Slight warmth on "Good evening" and "The table is yours", flat and dry on "I don't have a bad night."
TTS: text2speech_v2 with variant: "elevenlabs". Generate each line as its own job and feed the job ids straight into audio_references on the matching seedance shot — no upload step needed. Match the voice already used for the in-game bank so the commercial and the product are the same person.
6. Cutdowns
15s
Shots 1 → 3 → 4 → 7 → 9 → 10. VO: "Good evening. Your table's been waiting. Seven seats. And someone always watching me. Croupier — the table is yours."
6s bumper (social / pre-roll)
Shot 3 (2s) → shot 5 (2s) → shot 10 (2s). VO: "Your table's been waiting."
9:16 social
Reframe on Vera centre. Shots 1 and 7 need regenerating vertically — do not centre-crop the 21:9, you lose the pit boss entirely on shot 7. Burn captions in; assume sound off.
7. Music and sound
0:00–0:07 — sub-bass swell, room tone, sconce clicks. No melody.
0:07–0:16 — a single upright bass pulse enters, roughly 70bpm. Sparse brushed snare.
0:16–0:22 — everything drops out under the pit boss line except one sustained string.
0:22–0:30 — the pulse returns with a low piano figure, resolves on the logo.
Reference: the restraint of a Rolex or Bottega spot, not a casino ad. The most expensive sound in the spot is silence at 0:19.
8. On-screen text and compliance
Because this runs under an MGA licence, the copy has to stay clean. Baked into the board above:
18+ visible on the end card, and persistent in the corner where the placement requires it
Play responsibly plus the operator's RG link on the end card
Licence line on the end card
No implication that play is risk-free, guaranteed, or a way to make money
No suggestion that skill or the AI dealer improves your odds
Do not target or feature anyone who reads as under 25
Claims used in the spot that must stay factually true to the build:
"Seven seats" — the table plays seven boxes
"Blackjack pays 3:2 / dealer stands on all 17s" — matches the felt and the engine
"Every hand supervised" — keep this pointed at the pit boss and fairness, and have legal confirm the wording maps to what you actually certify (RNG certification, hand history)
Run the final copy past whoever holds the licence before you ship. The line most likely to get a note is "someone always watching me" — it is a fairness claim, so it needs to be one you can evidence.

FANTEAM LAUNCH — 30s Commercial Structure
Working title: "Every Second Counts" Concept: Real sport is fast. Your fantasy team is faster. Pick. Play. Win. Now. Format: 30 seconds · built from 8 beats (7 Higgsfield clips + end card) · 9:16 and 16:9 safe Tone: Adrenaline, stadium-scale, neon-on-dark, instant gratification



Higgsfield ground rules (read first)
Higgsfield clips run ~5 seconds — the 30s spot is 7 generated clips + 1 end card, with several clips trimmed to 2–4s in the edit to force the pace. Generate long, cut short.
One camera move per clip. Stacked moves render messy. The move is chosen per beat below.
Set aspect ratio in the app, not the prompt. Best dual-crop approach: generate every clip twice (9:16 and 16:9) with the same prompt + seed style, OR generate 16:9 and keep all action dead-center for the vertical crop. Framing notes per shot below.
Prompt order that works: Camera move → Subject → Action → Setting → Lighting → Lens/style → Mood. The prompts below follow it.
Keep a consistent look token in every prompt so clips cut together. Use the REALISM TOKEN: "shot on ARRI Alexa with 35mm anamorphic lens, natural color grade, real broadcast floodlighting, authentic skin texture, sweat and fabric detail, photorealistic live-action footage, subtle handheld shake"
Making it look REAL, not animated
The #1 cause of the "animated" look is stylization words in the prompt. Rules:

Ban these words from every prompt: neon, glowing, holographic, particles, cinematic, epic, dissolve, magical. They all bias the model toward CGI/game-trailer output.
Describe it like a camera operator, not a VFX artist. "Broadcast footage," "documentary style," "handheld," "caught on camera," "match-day coverage" all pull toward realism.
Add imperfection. Real footage has flaws: "slight motion blur," "lens flare from floodlights," "grain," "sweat," "grass stains," "breath visible in cold air." Perfect = fake.
Engine choice matters most. Inside Higgsfield, switch the generation engine to Veo 3.1 or Kling for live-action realism — the house style leans stylized. For the fan character, generate reference stills with Soul 2.0 (photorealism flagship) first.
Never ask the AI to render UI, numbers, or graphics. Generate clean live-action; add every point counter, notification, and brand color as an overlay in post (CapCut/After Effects). That's also where your brand teal/orange comes in — as a grade and graphics layer, not in the prompt.
If the engine supports negative prompts, add: "no CGI, no 3D render, no animation, no cartoon, no video game graphics."

Making it look REAL, not animated
The #1 cause of the "animated" look is stylization words in the prompt. Rules:
